text: Robert “Bob” Guy Walls (8 June 1927 – 11 November 1999) was a painter born in Upper Hutt, New Zealand. After completing his education at Wellington College, he worked for the Union Steamship Company, spending 17 years from 1943 to 1960, including 12 years at sea as a purser on ships trading primarily between New Zealand and Canada, and serving as a shipping representative in Tonga and the Cook Islands. It was during this period that he began painting as a hobby. In 1960, he moved to London and studied at the Chelsea School of Art from 1960 to 1963. His first solo exhibition took place in 1964 at the Drian Galleries in London. He painted full-time for many years, alongside some lecturing and teaching. By the 1970s, due to financial insecurity from relying on an artist’s income, he sought employment and worked briefly at the Foreign Office before joining the British Museum, where he served as a curator in the Prehistoric and Romano-British Departments until 1992. During his time at the museum, he was involved in the arrangements for the famous Lindow Man and in the display of the Vindolanda Tablets, the earliest written materials discovered in Britain. Walls held numerous exhibitions across Europe, the United Kingdom, and New Zealand, and his works are held in various public and private collections, including those of the Contemporary Art Society and the New Zealand National Gallery. He used a range of media, such as oils, watercolour, pastels, and gouache, with his paintings typically depicting land, sea, and townscapes, the landscapes mainly featuring Yorkshire, Scotland, Spain, and New Zealand. Walls resided in London for most of his adult life with his partner, John McLeod.
